name: Emeka Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Emeka. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartley's Foodstore on the high street in Dunmoor, a family supermarket, not one of the big chains. Mr Hartley opens up at seven and I'm in at half past, doing the newspapers, the milk and then the till until three, with stacking in between. I like that it's a proper shop where you know the customers and the boss knows your name. What wears me out is lifting the drinks deliveries on my own on a Monday, my back's not what it was at nineteen.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a small flat over the barber's with my fiancée Grace, who works at the bakery two doors down. We're getting married at our church next September, so every spare pound goes to that. Savings are about two weeks, honestly, and apart from Hartley's there's only a petrol station shop in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, a lot of noise from people who've never done a day's work on a shop floor. I'd say it at church and to the regulars. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't help much, because AI was never my worry. My worry is the big discount chain building on the bypass, opening next spring. If they take Hartley's customers, Mr Hartley can't keep four of us on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and work as hard as I can, so if Mr Hartley has to choose, he chooses me. I'd ask if I can take on the ordering when Mrs Hartley steps back. And Grace and I would keep putting forty a week into the wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an old kind of anxious. Small shops have always had to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the wedding if your hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, God willing, just with a smaller do. Grace's family would help, and so would mine. We'd make it work without borrowing, I won't start married life in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think hard work is enough to keep your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's always been enough at Hartley's. Mr Hartley kept his dad's staff through two recessions. A family business looks after the people who look after it.

He'd say it at **church** and to regular customers, not online.
think: His real worry is the **discount chain** opening on the bypass next spring.
If customers leave, Mr Hartley can't keep **four staff** on.
do: **Work** as hard as he can so Mr Hartley **chooses him** if cuts come.
**Ask** to take over the **ordering** when Mrs Hartley steps back.
**Put** **£40 a week** into the wedding fund with Grace.
feel: **Anxious**, in the old way of a **small shop** fighting to survive.
S0.quote: A family business looks after the people who look after it.
fieldNote: His threat is **competition** from a chain, not technology.
He trusts **loyalty** and hard work to protect him.
The **wedding** sets his money priorities, with no borrowing allowed.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hartley to hand over the ordering when Mrs Hartley steps back
Put forty pounds a week into the September wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no stopping progress, but there's such a thing as going too far. A shop without people isn't a shop. I'd say that to Mr Hartley and at the men's breakfast at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big chains use all this to undercut us even more. Their ordering and their prices get done by computers, so they can go cheaper. I won't touch these AI things, so if Mr Hartley wants them, he'll need someone younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and see what Mr Hartley does, because he's careful with new things too. I'd talk to my uncle Joseph about labouring for his building firm on Saturdays, to have something behind me. I wouldn't ask the government for anything, that's not how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground is shifting a bit under the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Hartley would need someone younger for AI. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. My cousin's lad is seventeen and he's on his phone all day, he'd pick it up in a week. But Mr Hartley knows I'm reliable, and that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Saturday labouring with your uncle look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carrying blocks and mixing cement on house extensions, fifty pounds a day cash in hand, well, declared. It's hard on the back but it's honest work. And a building site still needs people for a good while yet.

He'd say it to his boss and at the **church breakfast**.

feel: **Uneasy**, as if the **ground** under the shop is shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, and the people in charge should never have let it happen this fast. Somebody should be putting the brakes on. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Hartley's might hang on a few years because it's small and Mr Hartley hates gadgets. But by 2031, when the robots come, the chain on the bypass will be all robots and cheaper than anything. Then Hartley's closes and I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time with my uncle Joseph on the building side as soon as I could, to learn a trade while there's still time. Grace and I would move the wedding to the church hall with tea and sandwiches. And we'd stay in the flat and cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray about it, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building work is hands-on too. Doesn't the same thing happen there by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but houses are all different, aren't they, every wall's a bit crooked. I think a robot will find a supermarket shelf a lot easier than an old house in my town. That's my bet anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I'd run out of everything else, and I'd hate it. I'd rather Grace's dad found me work at his garage. Family first, then the church, then the state.

say: This is **reckless**, and those in charge should be putting on the **brakes**.
He'd say it at **church** and to anyone who'd listen.
think: Hartley's may last a few years, but by **2031** the chain's **robots** win.
He expects the shop to **close** and his job to go.
do: **Join** uncle Joseph's **building firm** full-time to learn a trade.
**Move** the wedding to the **church hall** with tea and sandwiches.
**Cut** all other spending and stay in the flat.
feel: **Alarmed**, praying about it and still **lying awake**.

fieldNote: He bets that **old houses** are harder for robots than shelves.

The **wedding** shrinks but still goes ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, so let's get young people into proper apprenticeships now, not more courses on screens. I'd say it to Mr Hartley and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd hang on at Hartley's too long. I'm not good at leaving things. But five years means maybe I can do a bricklaying apprenticeship before the robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle Joseph to take me on as a proper apprentice in the second year, after the wedding. In the first year I'd keep Hartley's and do Saturdays with him. We'd still have the wedding as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a path. Like walking in fog but you can see the next lamp post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at leaving things. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been at Hartley's since I was eighteen, Mr Hartley gave me a chance when nobody else would. Leaving feels like letting him down. But I can't feed a family on loyalty if the shop closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bricklaying apprenticeship pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than the shop at first, maybe a lot less. That's the hard bit with a wedding just done. Grace says we'll manage on her bakery wage for a year if we have to.

He'd raise it with Mr Hartley and at church.

steps.text: Keep the Hartley's job through the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no need for panic or handouts. People should learn a trade and get on with it. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably stay at Hartley's for most of those years, if it's still open. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots reach the shop floor around 2039, and maybe I'd have kids by then. That's the bit that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change nothing this year except the wedding and saving. In a few years I'd look at the apprenticeship, once I see how my cousin Daniel gets on with his. I'd keep doing Saturdays with uncle Joseph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little worry about my future children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see how Daniel gets on. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he's earning more than me after three years, and he's not broken his back. Then I'd go. I need to see it with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hartley's in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Mr Hartley will be retired, and his son doesn't want the shop. So either it's sold or it closes, robots or no robots. I've known that a while really.

People should learn a **trade** and get on with it.

He worries about **future children** when robots arrive in 2039.
do: **Change nothing** this year except the **wedding** and savings.
**Watch** how cousin Daniel's **apprenticeship** goes before deciding.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small worry about **future children**.
S4.quote: My boss Mr Hartley will be retired, and his son doesn't want the shop.
fieldNote: He admits the shop's future was **shaky** before AI came up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be starting married life with no job and no trade. What would help is real apprenticeships with a wage you can live on, not handouts. And for small shops like Hartley's to get a fair chance against the chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a shop means to a town. When Hartley's closes for the day, Dunmoor high street goes dark, and no robot is going to keep the lights on for the old folk.

headlineQuote: I'd be starting married life with no job and no trade.
portrait: Emeka, 27, has worked at **Hartley's Foodstore**, a family supermarket in Dunmoor, since he was eighteen.
He's engaged to Grace, a **bakery** worker, and every spare pound goes to their September **wedding**.
Traditional and cautious, he never uses AI and trusts **family, church** and hard work.
He sees a **building trade** with his uncle as his way out, but loyalty holds him back.
He is **anxious** in slow worlds and **alarmed** once AGI arrives within five years.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, starting married life with **no job** and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships** with a living wage, not **handouts**.
A **fair chance** for small shops against the chains.
